title: From switching devices to chips
alt: A vacuum-tube envelope, a three-terminal transistor and an integrated chip illustrate increasing integration. They are schematic symbols of construction, not to scale.
caption: Switching technology changed from separate large devices to many circuit elements integrated on one chip.

title: Different forms, different roles
alt: Original outlines show a rack, a desktop screen, a laptop and a handheld device. Size and shape do not determine whether a computer acts as a server or a client.
caption: A form factor describes physical packaging. Server, workstation and embedded controller describe roles.

title: Data paths and control paths
alt: The control unit sends dashed command paths to input, storage, ALU and output. Solid arrows carry input to storage, storage to ALU and output, and ALU results back to storage.
caption: Solid arrows carry data; dashed arrows indicate commands. The CPU includes the control unit and ALU. Storage remains a separate functional unit in this model.

title: Working memory and persistent storage
alt: Programs and data move from auxiliary storage into main memory for CPU use. Main RAM loses ordinary state without power; nonvolatile storage retains its recorded state.
caption: Loading is a transfer between two different stores. Nonvolatile storage retains data without power; it still needs backup against loss or failure.

title: Bits, patterns and a byte
alt: A binary tree doubles from two one-bit choices to four two-bit choices. Eight bit cells form one byte, with 256 possible patterns and unsigned values 0 to 255.
caption: Each independent bit doubles the pattern count. Eight bits give 256 patterns, not a greatest unsigned value of 256.

title: Group from the radix point
alt: The same binary pattern 101101.101 is grouped as 101 101 point 101 for octal 55.5 and as 0010 1101 point 1010 for hexadecimal 2D.A. Only outer padding zeros are added.
caption: Three binary digits select one octal digit; four select one hexadecimal digit. Group separately on each side of the point, padding only the outer ends.

title: The meaning comes from the format
alt: Data branches into character codes and numeric formats. Numeric formats branch into decimal digit codes and binary formats, with fixed point and floating point under binary.
caption: A bit pattern has no intrinsic character or numeric meaning. The selected format determines how those bits are interpreted.

title: A character code is a lookup
alt: The Latin capital letter A is U+0041 in Unicode and 0x41 in ASCII. Its UTF-8 byte is hexadecimal 41, binary 01000001. A grid uses high nibble 4 and low nibble 1 to locate hexadecimal 41.
caption: Split the byte into two nibbles to locate its hexadecimal code. A code point and an encoded byte sequence are different concepts.

title: Decimal digits packed into nibbles
alt: Decimal 672 becomes BCD nibbles 0110, 0111, 0010. A common signed packed representation is hexadecimal 67 2C for positive 672. EBCDIC-style zoned positive digits are F6 F7 C2, with the final zone holding the sign.
caption: In this explicitly chosen convention, C is a positive sign and D a negative sign. Packed 67 2C uses two bytes; zoned F6 F7 C2 uses three. Sign codes depend on the format.

title: Two signed four-bit interpretations
alt: For four bits, sign-magnitude uses 0000 for plus zero and 1000 for minus zero, spanning minus 7 to plus 7. Two’s complement uses one zero, spans minus 8 to plus 7, and gives 1000 the value minus 8.
caption: The same 1000 pattern means −0 in sign-magnitude and −8 in two’s complement. Two’s complement uses all 16 patterns for 16 distinct integer values.

title: Three ways to shift right
alt: Starting with 10010110, logical right shift inserts zero to give 01001011; arithmetic right shift repeats one to give 11001011; rotate right wraps the discarded zero to give 01001011. Rotation differs from a shift even when this example’s results match.
caption: Eight-bit operations, shifted once. Logical fill is zero; arithmetic right fill repeats the sign; rotation wraps the outgoing bit. Left shifts can discard significant bits and overflow.

title: Trace an instruction through the CPU
alt: Step 1: PC sends an instruction address to memory. Step 2: memory returns the instruction to IR, which feeds the decoder. Step 3: the decoder directs registers and ALU. Step 4: an operand is read and the ALU result is written back. PC advances or branches separately.
caption: PC holds an instruction address; IR holds the fetched instruction. The decoder directs an operation, while the ALU operates on data. Solid paths move addresses/data; the dashed path carries control.

title: Timing and three bus roles
alt: Two rising edges delimit one clock period. CPU sends addresses and read/write control to memory; a bidirectional data path carries values. A 100 MHz clock has a 10 nanosecond period.
caption: Clock cycles provide timing. Address, data and control have different roles; one cycle need not equal one instruction or one useful bus transfer.

title: Two ways to retain a working bit
alt: A conceptual DRAM cell connects a data line through a selected transistor to a capacitor, whose charge must be refreshed. SRAM uses feedback to retain state while powered. Both are volatile.
caption: A capacitor stores charge in DRAM; feedback maintains a state in SRAM while power is supplied. These are conceptual models, not transistor-level manufacturing layouts.

title: An address selects a location
alt: Address 2 enters a decoder, which selects row 2 from a four-row memory. The selected stored value is hexadecimal A6; the address 2 and data A6 are different.
caption: This four-location memory has two address bits and one byte per location: 2² × 8 = 32 bits total. The address is not the byte stored there.

title: An instruction contains fields
alt: An illustrative sixteen-bit instruction has a four-bit opcode, a four-bit register field and an eight-bit operand field. The format is a teaching example, not a particular ISA.
caption: Instruction layout is defined by the ISA. An operand field can encode a literal, register or address information; it is not always a final memory address.

title: Follow the dereference
alt: Instruction field A is 40. Immediate mode uses operand 40; direct mode reads M[40], which is 700; indirect mode follows 700 to M[700], which is 12. Indexed addressing with R equal to 3 selects address 43.
caption: Each arrow through a memory box is a dereference. Immediate 40, direct 700 and indirect 12 are three different operands from the same instruction field.

title: Read the gate symbol
alt: AND has a flat input side, OR a curved input side and XOR an extra curved line. NOT is a triangle with an output bubble. NAND is AND with a bubble; NOR is OR with a bubble. A bubble means inversion.
caption: Gate shape identifies the operation. A small output bubble negates it. Compare the connections with the truth table above; the extra input-side curve distinguishes XOR from OR.

title: Feedback stores a state
alt: Two cross-coupled NAND gates form an active-low SR latch. S_n enters the upper gate and R_n the lower. Q feeds the lower feedback input; Q-bar feeds the upper feedback input. S_n=0 R_n=1 sets Q; S_n=1 R_n=0 resets Q; both one hold; both zero is forbidden.
caption: Active-low NAND SR latch, matching the source’s NAND convention. The suffix _n marks a low-active input. S_n=R_n=1 holds; 01 sets; 10 resets; 00 forces both outputs high and is forbidden.

title: Construct XOR from two cases
alt: Input A and inverted B feed the upper AND gate. Inverted A and B feed the lower AND gate. The two AND outputs feed OR, so Y equals A AND NOT B OR NOT A AND B.
caption: XOR is true in exactly the two unequal-input cases. The labeled negations are part of the wiring; omitting either changes the function.

title: A full adder from two half adders
alt: Half adder 1 takes A and B and gives intermediate sum s1 and carry c1. Half adder 2 takes s1 and carry-in, and gives sum and carry c2. OR combines c1 and c2 into carry-out.
caption: Each half adder computes XOR for its sum and AND for its carry. OR combines the two carry paths: carry-out = AB OR (carry-in AND (A XOR B)).

title: Buffering at different levels
alt: CPU registers connect through primary and secondary cache to main memory, and then through a disk-cache role to storage. A miss continues down the hierarchy; a hit returns earlier. A disk cache may use part of main RAM.
caption: Each buffer bridges levels with different access costs. A disk cache may occupy main RAM rather than being a separate physical chip. Arrows show a read lookup sequence, not all coherence traffic.

title: Distribute successive addresses
alt: Four memory banks contain addresses 0,4,8; 1,5,9; 2,6,10; and 3,7,11. A controller can overlap operations across banks. The bank number is address modulo four in this simplified word-addressed model.
caption: Successive word addresses go to different banks in this simplified mapping. Interleaving can improve sustained throughput; it does not divide every access latency by four.

title: A stall delays following work
alt: A three-stage pipeline takes a bubble when instruction I2 cannot execute. In cycles 1 through 6, I1 runs F D E; I2 runs F D wait E; I3 runs F wait D E. A deeper pipeline splits stages but still must handle dependencies.
caption: F = fetch, D = decode, E = execute; “wait” is a bubble. Throughput falls when a stage cannot advance. Splitting stages in a super-pipeline does not remove dependencies.

title: Track, sector, head and cylinder
alt: A disk surface has concentric tracks and sector wedges. The read/write head sits over one track. A second view marks the same-radius tracks on three surfaces as one cylinder.
caption: A track circles one recording surface; sectors divide recording regions. Matching-radius tracks across surfaces form the simplified cylinder model. The drawing is not to scale.

title: Records, blocks and unused space
alt: A 512-byte block contains five 100-byte records and 12 unused bytes. A second schematic shows variable-length recorded blocks separated by interblock gaps, distinct from unused space inside a block.
caption: Five 100-byte records fit in 512 bytes without spanning. Unused bytes inside an allocated block differ from physical interblock gaps; the recording model must be stated.

title: Three parts of a disk read
alt: A timeline separates head movement (seek), waiting for rotation and transferring the requested bytes. At 7200 rpm, a rotation is 8.333 milliseconds and average rotational waiting is 4.167 milliseconds.
caption: Seek positions the head, rotation brings the sector under it, and transfer moves bytes. Controller overhead is added separately when specified. Segment lengths here are illustrative.

title: From physical input to output
alt: A document scanner produces image data, memory and the CPU process it, and a printer produces a physical page. Input and output are relative to the computer.
caption: A multifunction device can contain all three stages. Scanning supplies image data; recognition or editing is processing; printing is output.

title: One press, several contact transitions
alt: A raw key-contact waveform briefly toggles after the press and then stays high. A debounced waveform changes once after a settling delay. This differs from deliberate held-key repeat.
caption: Contact bounce can create several electrical transitions for one press. A debounce method waits or filters; the exact delay depends on the design.

title: Recognition and capture differ
alt: OCR recognizes the printed glyph A; OMR reads a filled option position; a barcode reader decodes bars; MICR senses magnetic characters; a scanner captures pixels before any recognition.
caption: OCR reads character shapes; OMR reads marks at known positions; MICR senses magnetic characters. Capturing an image is different from identifying its contents.

title: Relative motion or absolute position
alt: A mouse reports a movement of plus 5 in x and minus 2 in y. A touch or digitizer surface identifies a point with absolute x,y coordinates inside its bounds. These are different input models.
caption: A mouse normally reports movement relative to a previous position. A touch panel or digitizer can locate a point on its surface; sensing technology and coordinate interpretation are separate.

title: A glyph is a grid of samples
alt: A five-by-seven binary pixel grid forms an A from 35 samples. RGB pixels can use eight bits each for red, green and blue, totaling 24 bits or three bytes per pixel.
caption: This original 5 × 7 glyph contains 35 samples. Resolution counts samples; color depth counts bits per sample. At 24 bits/pixel, a packed RGB image uses three bytes per pixel.

title: Pins transfer ink through a ribbon
alt: An impact print head pushes pins toward an ink ribbon, which contacts paper. Pin positions form dots. It contrasts with inkjet droplets and laser-transferred toner.
caption: Mechanical impact transfers ink from the ribbon to the paper. Inkjet and laser printing form marks by different mechanisms; they do not strike an ink ribbon.

title: A path drawing or a projected image
alt: A plotter pen follows an x-y path to mark a physical surface. A projector sends an image using light onto a screen. Both are output, but they produce different physical results.
caption: A plotter controls a tool path. A projector casts light. A shared digital drawing can be represented by either kind of output without making their mechanisms identical.

title: Who moves the block?
alt: Programmed transfer routes data from device through the CPU to memory. DMA routes data between a device controller and memory after CPU setup, then notifies the CPU on completion.
caption: DMA reduces per-byte CPU instructions. The CPU still sets up the transfer and handles completion; bus and memory resources are still used.

title: Star, cascade and daisy chain
alt: A star connects devices to one hub. A cascade connects a hub to another hub, with devices branching from them. A daisy chain connects onward through devices, with a terminator when that interface requires one.
caption: These are connection patterns, not interchangeable USB modes. USB uses hubs in a tiered star; a legacy SCSI daisy chain requires termination under its specified rules.

title: Read integer and fraction digits differently
alt: Repeated division of 26 by two yields remainders 0,1,0,1,1, read upward as 11010. Repeated multiplication of 0.625 by two yields integer parts 1,0,1, read downward as .101.
caption: Integer remainders are read from the final division back upward. Fractional integer parts are read in the order generated. The result is 11010.101₂.

title: A recurring remainder creates recurring bits
alt: Starting with decimal fraction 0.1, repeated multiplication by two emits bits 0,0,0,1,1 and leaves remainders 0.2,0.4,0.8,0.6,0.2. The remainder 0.2 repeats, so subsequent bits repeat 0011.
caption: 0.1₁₀ = 0.000110011…₂. Once the same fractional remainder returns, the subsequent digits repeat. Finite storage must round or truncate this expansion.

title: Normalize, then store the fields
alt: Binary 1010.1 normalizes to 1.0101 times two cubed. For binary32 the sign is zero, biased exponent is 130 and the stored fraction begins 0101. Binary32 has field widths 1,8,23; binary64 has 1,11,52 and bias 1023.
caption: For normal finite values, the leading 1 is implicit. Binary32 has 24 significant binary digits including that 1; binary64 has 53. Zero/subnormal and all-ones exponent fields need separate rules.

title: Precision and range are different limits
alt: With three significant decimal digits, 1.234 rounds to 1.23. Subtracting the rounded 1.234 and 1.233 gives zero instead of the exact 0.001. Adding 1 to 1.00 million can lose the small term. Underflow concerns tiny magnitudes near zero; overflow concerns excessive magnitude of either sign.
caption: Illustrative three-significant-digit decimal arithmetic. Cancellation and lost small terms concern precision. Underflow concerns tiny magnitudes near zero, not simply any value below a signed minimum.
